screens.title: Template Metaprogramming (TMP) Basics
screens.subtitle: Using C++ templates to compute, specialize, and enforce policies at compile time

narration.text: Welcome. In this lesson you will learn what Template Metaprogramming is, why engineers use it, and how simple examples like a compile-time factorial work. Template Metaprogramming treats the compiler as a computation engine: templates instantiate and evaluate during compilation to produce pre-computed values or specialized code paths. That matters because when you shift work to compile time you can improve runtime speed, catch type errors early, and generate bespoke code for different types. For example, a recursive template can compute factorial values before the program starts, removing the need to compute them at runtime. We will also compare that older recursive template style with modern constexpr functions and C++17's if constexpr which lets you write clearer conditional compile-time branches. Finally you will see how type traits like std::is_integral and SFINAE patterns such as std::enable_if let you tailor overloads and enforce constraints. As you follow the code walkthroughs and the hands-on starter, notice where the compiler is responsible for work and ask yourself whether a computation benefits from being done once at compile time or left to run repeatedly at runtime.

keyIdea.title: Core idea
keyIdea.text: TMP uses C++ templates and compile-time evaluation to produce pre-computed values and specialized code, improving performance and type safety.

Template Metaprogramming (TMP) Basics

Learn how templates and compile-time features produce pre-computed results and specialized code paths. We’ll explore recursive templates, type traits, SFINAE, and the modern if constexpr alternative.

Orientation

This chapter pairs short code walkthroughs with conceptual visuals. Expect live-coding examples for factorial and conditional templates, plus a hands-on starter to practice if constexpr with type traits.

Visual Concept
Compile-time
Templates and constexpr evaluated by the compiler. Produces constants or specialized code.
Runtime
Regular functions and loops executed when the program runs. Flexible but costs time each run.
Example: Factorial
Recursive template instantiation yields Factorial<5> as a compile-time constant. A constexpr function can compute it at compile time when its input is constant.
Compiler as evaluator
Explore Key Topics
Recursive Templates
Use recursion and specialization to compute constants like factorial or Fibonacci at compile time.
Type Traits
Ask questions about types using std::is_integral, std::is_pointer, and others to shape code paths.
if constexpr
A clean C++17 way to write compile-time branches that discard invalid code for other types.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you'll be able to do after this lesson

narration.text: By the end of this lesson you will be able to define Template Metaprogramming and explain why it is used, implement simple recursive templates that compute values at compile time, and use type traits to ask questions about types. You will also be able to apply if constexpr to write cleaner compile-time conditional logic. Each objective pairs a skill with why it matters: defining TMP helps you reason about when the compiler should do work instead of the C P U at runtime; building recursive templates shows how base cases and specialization terminate compile-time recursion safely; using type traits enables conditional code paths and safer overloads; and using if constexpr reduces complexity compared to SFINAE in many cases. These skills let you write code that is both faster at runtime and safer at compile time, and they prepare you to read and maintain libraries that rely on TMP patterns. As you practice, notice how compile-time choices change the final binary and how that affects debugging and error messages.

keyIdea.title: Goal
keyIdea.text: Understand, write, and apply basic TMP constructs such as recursive templates, type traits, and if constexpr for safer, faster C++.

narration.text: Template Metaprogramming is a style of programming where templates are used as a compile-time language. You write templates that the compiler instantiates and evaluates, producing values and specialized code before the program runs. The practical motivations are threefold: performance because repeated runtime work can be done once at compile time; type safety because type constraints and code generation happen during compilation; and code generation because the compiler can produce different implementations for different types. A common misconception is that TMP is only for exotic library authors. In fact, basic TMP patterns like compile-time constants and simple type traits are useful in application code when you need zero-overhead abstractions. Another misconception is that constexpr always replaces TMP; while constexpr functions are often clearer for value computation, classic TMP structures force compile-time evaluation and are essential when type-level programming or specialization is required. Example: computing a factorial using a recursive template yields a constant the program can use directly. Key takeaway: TMP moves work earlier so the runtime becomes faster and more predictable, but it also shifts complexity to compilation and error messages. Think about whether pre-computing a result gives a measurable runtime benefit before choosing TMP.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: TMP uses template instantiation and compile-time evaluation to produce constants and specialized code paths before runtime.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.4 › What is TMP?
Core Concept

Template Metaprogramming

A programming approach where templates act as a compile-time computation language. Use it to produce constants or specialized code before runtime.

Motivation: Performance
Pre-compute values so the final binary runs faster without recomputing the same results.
Motivation: Type Safety
Enforce constraints and generate type-specific code at compile time, catching mistakes earlier.
Common Misconception
TMP is not always required; prefer constexpr for simple value computations and if constexpr for conditional branches when possible.
Key Takeaway

Use TMP when compile-time specialization or type-level computation provides clear runtime or safety benefits; otherwise prefer clearer constexpr solutions.

Analogy & Example
Think of TMP as a build step that bakes answers into the binary. Below is a minimal conceptual example of what a recursive template looks like (the full code walkthrough appears later).
// Conceptual form
template <int N>
struct Factorial {
  static const long long value = N * Factorial<N - 1>::value;
};

template <>
struct Factorial<0> {
  static const long long value = 1;
};

// Factorial<5> yields a compile-time constant 120
Notice the base specialization that stops recursion. Missing it can lead to infinite template instantiation and compile-time errors. That is a common debugging point in TMP.

screens.title: Compile-time vs. Runtime
screens.subtitle: How work is shifted and what changes in the final program

narration.text: Understanding how compile-time and runtime differ is essential when deciding whether to use TMP. At runtime, code is executed by the C P U each time a function is called or a loop runs. At compile time, the compiler instantiates templates and evaluates constexpr expressions, producing concrete types and constants embedded in the binary. The practical process is: you write templates or constexpr functions, the compiler instantiates templates or evaluates constexpr when possible, and the linker produces an executable that contains the pre-computed values or specialized functions. A simple example: computing a lookup table at compile time using nested templates or constexpr arrays means the program reads the table directly rather than computing it repeatedly at runtime. A common misconception is that compile-time work is free; it is not — it increases compile time and can make error messages more complex. Use TMP for frequently-executed or performance-critical paths where compile-time specialization yields better runtime performance. In tests, compare a version that computes a value at runtime against a version that uses compile-time constants and measure whether the complexity trade-off is justified.

keyIdea.title: Process
keyIdea.text: Compile-time evaluation shifts computation to the compiler, producing specialized code and constants embedded in the binary instead of repeated runtime work.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.4 › Compile-time vs. Runtime
Process Flow

Where work happens

Write
Templates or constexpr functions in source code.
Compile
Compiler instantiates templates and evaluates constexpr expressions, producing concrete types and values.
Run
Program uses pre-computed values or specialized code for faster execution.
Why it matters

Shift expensive, repeated computations to compile time only when the benefit outweighs increased compile time and potential complexity.

Concrete Example
Imagine a polynomial evaluator used in a tight loop. If coefficients and degree are known at compile time, the compiler can unroll and specialize evaluation logic so the loop runs faster. Otherwise, repeated runtime evaluation may dominate cost. Test both approaches and prefer compile-time work for hot paths.
Common Mistake
Overusing TMP for non-critical code increases compile time and makes maintenance harder. Prefer clear code unless profiling shows runtime cost.
Check Your Understanding
When would you prefer constexpr over TMP templates? Answer: prefer constexpr for value computation when type-level specialization is not required.

screens.title: Recursive Factorial with Templates
screens.subtitle: How Factorial<N>::value is computed at compile time

narration.text: Let's walk through a classic recursive template example: the Factorial struct. The template defines a primary template that computes N times Factorial of N minus one, while a specialization for zero returns 1 and stops recursion. When you ask for Factorial ::value the compiler instantiates Factorial, which depends on Factorial, and so on until it reaches Factorial ::value which is 1. The compiler multiplies back up during compilation and makes the final value available as a static constant. A concrete walkthrough: Factorial requires Factorial, which requires Factorial, continuing until Factorial. The base specialization is essential; without it instantiation never terminates. Note that this template struct method forces compile-time evaluation regardless of how you use the value. Contrast this with a constexpr function which may compute at compile time only when given constant inputs. A common debugging point is mis-typed specialization syntax or forgetting to specialize the base case. Always test with small values first and inspect compiler diagnostics to trace instantiation depth. After this walkthrough, you should be able to both read and write a simple recursive template with a terminating specialization.

keyIdea.title: Recursive instantiation
keyIdea.text: The compiler instantiates templates recursively until it finds a base specialization, then computes the final value during compilation.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.4 › Recursive Factorial
Code Walkthrough

Factorial as a template struct

#include <iostream>

// Base case for Factorial
template <int N>
struct Factorial {
  static const long long value = N * Factorial<N - 1>::value;
};

// Specialization for Factorial<0>
template <>
struct Factorial<0> {
  static const long long value = 1;
};

// Usage: Factorial<5>::value is computed at compile time
This code forces compile-time computation. The base specialization Factorial<0> stops recursion. If the base were missing, the compiler would produce an instantiation-depth error.
Step-by-step instantiation
Request: Factorial<5>::value 1) Instantiate Factorial<5> which needs Factorial<4>::value 2) Instantiate Factorial<4> which needs Factorial<3>::value 3) Continue until Factorial<0> specialization is used and returns 1 4) Multiply back up: 1 * 1 * 2 * 3 * 4 * 5 = 120
Common Mistake
Forgetting the base case or mis-declaring the specialization causes non-terminating instantiation errors or deep template recursion diagnostics.
Pro Tip
Test with small N values and read instantiation traces to find which specialization the compiler selects.

screens.title: constexpr function vs. template struct
screens.subtitle: When to prefer constexpr and when templates force compile-time results

narration.text: Compare the template struct approach with a constexpr function for factorial. A constexpr function can be evaluated at compile time if given constant inputs; otherwise it executes at runtime like a normal function. The template struct approach, however, produces a compile-time constant unconditionally when requested as a template specialization. Practically, prefer a constexpr function when you want cleaner syntax and the choice of compile-time vs runtime evaluation depending on use. Use template structs when the computation or value must always be part of type-level programming or when you need compile-time constants available in contexts that require constant expressions, such as array sizes or template parameters. Example code shows a recursive constexpr function that returns 1 for zero and otherwise multiplies by a recursive call. A key misconception is that constexpr automatically guarantees compile-time work; the argument must be a compile-time constant. Another pitfall is relying on template structs for very deep recursions; compilers have instantiation depth limits that may require iterative constexpr solutions instead. After this comparison, you should be able to justify both approaches and choose the clearer, maintainable option when feasible.

keyIdea.title: Comparison
keyIdea.text: constexpr provides readable compile-time-capable functions; template structs guarantee compile-time values and are useful in type-level contexts.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.4 › constexpr vs Templates
constexpr example
constexpr long long factorial_constexpr(int n) {
  return (n == 0) ? 1 : n * factorial_constexpr(n - 1);
}

// Called with a compile-time constant, the compiler may evaluate this at compile time.
A constexpr function is clearer and often preferable when you want both readability and optional compile-time evaluation. Use it when arguments can be constant or when you prefer fewer template instantiations.
Template struct example
template <int N>
struct Factorial {
  static const long long value = N * Factorial<N - 1>::value;
};

template <>
struct Factorial<0> { static const long long value = 1; };

// Factorial<5>::value is always a compile-time constant
Use template structs when you need the value at the type level or require unconditional compile-time availability, such as template parameters or static asserts that need constants.
Misconception
Not every constexpr call is evaluated at compile time; the argument must be a compile-time constant for that to happen.
When to prefer which
Prefer constexpr for readability and optional compile-time evaluation; prefer template structs when type-level constants are required.

screens.title: Type Traits — Asking questions about types
screens.subtitle: How std::type_traits helps you write conditional templates

narration.text: Type traits are templates that encode information about types at compile time. The C++ standard's header ships many useful queries, such as std::is_integral, std::is_floating_point, and std::is_pointer. You use these traits to write conditional code: either by enabling overloads with SFINAE or by branching inside a function with if constexpr. For instance, std::is_integral<T>::value is true for integer types, letting you choose integer-specific logic. A common pitfall is testing for printable behavior using type traits; printing relies on operator overloads, not type identity. Use std::is_convertible to detect whether a type can convert to std::string when you want string-like handling. Another useful trait is std::is_same for exact type matches. Practical example: you may write templates that only participate in overload resolution when a trait is true, using std::enable_if. With modern C++, prefer if constexpr inside a single template for readability, but knowing traits is necessary because both SFINAE and if constexpr rely on these compile-time properties. Practice reading traits in library code to see how they steer instantiation and overload selection. Type Traits — Asking questions about types means traits express type properties at compile time and power conditional compilation using sfinae or if constexpr.. In practical terms, how std::type_traits helps you write conditional templates. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Type Traits
keyIdea.text: Traits express type properties at compile time and power conditional compilation using SFINAE or if constexpr.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.4 › Type Traits
Definition

What are type traits?

Compile-time predicates and utilities that report properties of types, like whether a type is integral or pointer, or whether it is convertible to another type.

Examples
std::is_integral<T>, std::is_pointer<T>, std::is_convertible<T, U>.
Use cases
Enable overloads, perform compile-time assertions, or branch code with if constexpr based on type properties.
Quick Example
#include <type_traits>

static_assert(std::is_integral<int>::value, "int is integral");
// std::is_integral<double>::value is false
Traits are the building blocks for conditional templates. They don’t perform operations themselves, they report properties so you can select appropriate code paths at compile time.

screens.title: SFINAE and std::enable_if
screens.subtitle: How substitution failure removes overloads without error

narration.text: SFINAE stands for Substitution Failure Is Not An Error. It describes a compiler behavior during template substitution: if instantiating a template parameter in a candidate overload would be invalid, that overload is discarded rather than producing a hard compile error. std::enable_if is a common SFINAE utility that conditionally provides a type member only when a boolean trait is true. The classic use is to enable one overload for integral types and another for non-integral types. For example, you can write two processNumber templates where the return type is present only when std::is_integral is true or false respectively. When a call is made, the compiler substitutes the template parameters; if enable_if fails to produce a type, that overload disappears from the overload set and the compiler selects the remaining candidate. A misconception is that SFINAE always provides clear diagnostics; in practice, SFINAE can make errors harder to interpret and code harder to read. That is one reason why C++17 introduced if constexpr as a clearer in-body alternative. Still, understanding SFINAE is essential for reading legacy libraries that use enable_if heavily. Practice by creating small overload pairs and observing which one the compiler selects given different argument types.

keyIdea.title: SFINAE principle
keyIdea.text: A failed substitution removes a template overload from consideration instead of causing a compilation error; std::enable_if commonly implements this behavior.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.4 › SFINAE & enable_if
Comparison

SFINAE via std::enable_if

#include <type_traits>
#include <iostream>

template <typename T>
typename std::enable_if<std::is_integral<T>::value, void>::type
processNumber(T value) { std::cout << "Processing integral number: " << value << std::endl; }

template <typename T>
typename std::enable_if<!std::is_integral<T>::value, void>::type
processNumber(T value) { std::cout << "Processing non-integral value: " << value << std::endl; }
When T is an integral type, the first overload is valid and the second fails substitution and is discarded. The opposite happens for non-integral types. This achieves compile-time selection without runtime checks.
Practical notes
SFINAE can obscure diagnostics and produce complex signatures. Prefer if constexpr when possible for clarity. Still, SFINAE remains important to understand for legacy code and finer-grained overload control.
Common Mistake
Placing enable_if in the wrong position (e.g., return type vs template parameter) can change overload resolution and is a frequent source of subtle bugs.

screens.title: if constexpr: modern compile-time branching
screens.subtitle: Write a single template body that compiles only valid branches

narration.text: C++17 introduced if constexpr to let you write compile-time branching inside a function body. The condition is evaluated at compile time, and only the true branch is instantiated; the false branches are discarded, avoiding compile errors for code that would be invalid for a given type. This is much clearer than SFINAE for many use cases. Consider a template modernProcessValue that checks std::is_integral for an integer branch, std::is_floating_point for floating-point, and a generic else for other types. When you call this function with an int, the compiler compiles only the integral branch and discards the others; if those other branches contained invalid operations for T, they would not cause compilation failure. Use if constexpr for readable, maintainable conditional compilation when branch validity depends solely on compile-time traits. A common mistake is writing runtime if where compile-time branching is needed; that will still compile but won't avoid invalid code instantiation. Practice by calling modernProcessValue with int, float, string, and a custom struct to observe which branches are compiled and which are discarded. if constexpr: modern compile-time branching means if constexpr evaluates conditions at compile time and instantiates only the true branch, simplifying conditional tmp logic.. In practical terms, write a single template body that compiles only valid branches. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: if constexpr
keyIdea.text: if constexpr evaluates conditions at compile time and instantiates only the true branch, simplifying conditional TMP logic.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.4 › if constexpr
Example
#include <iostream>
#include <type_traits>

template <typename T>
void modernProcessValue(T value) {
  if constexpr (std::is_integral<T>::value) {
    std::cout << "Modern: Processing integral number: " << value << std::endl;
  } else if constexpr (std::is_floating_point<T>::value) {
    std::cout << "Modern: Processing floating-point number: " << value << std::endl;
  } else {
    std::cout << "Modern: Processing other value: " << value << std::endl;
  }
}
Only the branch that matches T will be compiled. If the discarded branch contains expressions invalid for T, they do not cause errors because they are not instantiated.
Practice
Call modernProcessValue with int, float, string, and a custom struct to observe which branch is compiled. This exercise shows the clarity and robustness of if constexpr compared to SFINAE overloads.
Pro Tip
Prefer if constexpr inside a template when all branches are determined by compile-time traits; it reduces template proliferation and improves diagnostics.

screens.title: Starter: Implement printInfo with if constexpr
screens.subtitle: A live-coding style starter to practice type traits and if constexpr

narration.text: This hands-on starter asks you to implement a printInfo function template that behaves differently for numeric types and strings, using if constexpr and type traits. The idea is to use std::is_arithmetic to detect numeric types and print the value and its square. Then check whether the type is convertible to std::string using std::is_convertible or is exactly std::string to handle string-like types by printing length. For any other type, print a generic message. The starter code provides a small custom struct Point and an operator<< overload for easy printing. Focus on the branching logic inside printInfo: use if constexpr so only the matching branch is instantiated. A common pitfall is attempting to call string operations on a non-string type without guarding the call with if constexpr; that causes compilation errors because the expression would be instantiated even if not executed at runtime. Test printInfo with int, double, const char*, std::string, and Point to see each branch chosen. This exercise reinforces type traits, if constexpr, and the difference between convertible and exact type checks. Starter: Implement printInfo with if constexpr means implement printinfo using if constexpr, std::is_arithmetic, and string-convertible checks to route compile-time branches.. In practical terms, a live-coding style starter to practice type traits and if constexpr. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Practice task
keyIdea.text: Implement printInfo using if constexpr, std::is_arithmetic, and string-convertible checks to route compile-time branches.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.4 › printInfo Starter
Starter Code
#include <iostream>
#include <string>
#include <type_traits>

struct Point { int x, y; Point(int _x, int _y) : x(_x), y(_y) {} };
std::ostream& operator<<(std::ostream& os, const Point& p) { os << "Point(" << p.x << ", " << p.y << ")"; return os; }

// TODO: Define the printInfo function template here using if constexpr

int main() {
  printInfo(10);
  printInfo(3.14);
  printInfo("Hello C++!");
  printInfo(std::string("Template Metaprogramming"));
  printInfo(Point(1,2));
  printInfo(true);
  return 0;
}
Your task: implement printInfo with if constexpr and type traits. Use std::is_arithmetic<T> to detect numbers and std::is_convertible_v<T, std::string> or std::is_same_v for strings. Guard operations like .length() inside the appropriate compile-time branch to avoid compilation errors.
Hints & Mistakes
Hint
Use if constexpr (std::is_arithmetic<T>::value) { ... } else if constexpr (std::is_convertible_v<T, std::string>) { ... } else { ... }
Common Mistake
Calling .length() or string operations outside a guarded branch causes compilation errors because those expressions get instantiated for all template instantiations unless guarded by if constexpr.
Try this
After implementing, test with bool and a custom struct to verify branch selection and that no invalid code is compiled for non-string, non-numeric types.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: What to remember from TMP basics

narration.text: These concise cards capture the essential ideas to retain. First, Template Metaprogramming uses template instantiation and compile-time evaluation to produce constants and specialized code. Second, compile-time computation shifts work to the compiler, yielding faster runtime but longer compile times and different debugging trade-offs. Third, recursive templates implement compile-time loops and require base specializations to terminate; factorial and Fibonacci are classic examples. Keep these ideas in mind as you read and write TMP code: prefer clarity with constexpr and if constexpr when possible, and rely on type traits to make safe compile-time decisions. Understanding these core concepts helps you maintain libraries that use TMP and decide when to choose compile-time strategies for performance and type safety. Key Concepts means tmp, compile-time computation, and recursive templates are the foundation for compile-time specialization and safety.. In practical terms, what to remember from tmp basics. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Essentials
keyIdea.text: TMP, compile-time computation, and recursive templates are the foundation for compile-time specialization and safety.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.4 › Key Concepts
Template Metaprogramming
Use templates as a compile-time language to compute values and generate specialized code.
Compile-time Computation
Computation by the compiler yields pre-computed constants and optimized binaries.
Recursive Templates
Recursive instantiation with a base specialization implements compile-time loops and constants like factorial and Fibonacci.
Summary Takeaway

Use TMP selectively for performance and type-level needs; prefer constexpr and if constexpr for clarity when they meet requirements.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Tools & Techniques
screens.subtitle: Practical utilities to use in TMP

narration.text: Keep these tools in your mental toolkit. Type traits from report properties like integrality and convertibility and underpin conditional compilation. SFINAE and std::enable_if let you remove overloads when substitution fails, but they can make code harder to read. C++17's if constexpr provides a clearer way to write compile-time branches inside a single function body, instantiating only the valid branch. Remember to test with representative types so you observe which branches or overloads the compiler selects. Together, these techniques let you write safer, faster code when compile-time decisions are warranted. Reflect: when you next optimize a hot path, ask whether compile-time specialization will reduce runtime cost enough to offset compile-time complexity. In practical terms, practical utilities to use in tmp. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Tools
keyIdea.text: std::type_traits, std::enable_if (SFINAE), and if constexpr are the primary tools to implement conditional compile-time behavior.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.4 › Tools & Techniques
Type Traits
std::is_integral, std::is_convertible, std::is_pointer — the predicates used to decide compile-time behavior.
SFINAE / enable_if
Use to conditionally remove overloads. Powerful but can complicate diagnostics and readability.
if constexpr
Prefer for in-body compile-time branching. Only the true branch is instantiated, simplifying code and errors.
